title: Three Times the Hammer: How Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips Devour the Art Market
excerpt: Three auction houses dominate the global art market and define what art is worth. But who actually sets the price of beauty — and at what cost to culture?
content:
The air in London, New York and Geneva is heavy with the perfume of money. Three addresses, three institutions, one single objective: to nail down the value of beauty. Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips — the unholy trinity of a market that long ago stopped asking after meaning. Here, nobody argues over light and shadow anymore; they argue over provenance and margin. Welcome to the glamorous slaughterhouse of vanities, where art is no longer beheld but auctioned off.

The Cathedral of Capitalism

Step into the marble halls of these temples and you breathe in the dust of three centuries of unchallenged power. Traditional houses like the Dorotheum (founded 1707) or Lempertz (since 1798) may be older, yet the global hegemony of the Big Three defines today, ex cathedra, what counts as art and what is mere decoration. They no longer function merely as intermediaries, but as gatekeepers of a religion whose god lives in the vault.

The hammer price is not the result of free demand, but a calculated verdict on cultural relevance.

These three players have overheated the market so thoroughly that public institutions — the actual custodians of our cultural memory — long ago lost any chance at the paddle. While a museum has to haggle over every cent, private collectors clench their fists inside their velvet-gloved pockets. The result is a perverse inversion: artworks created for the people vanish into climate-controlled bunkers, out of sight, toward the asset column.

The Manufacture of Value

We are told that auction houses create price transparency. That they are the informational backbone for insurance valuations, bank loans, inheritance tax. A soothing myth for economists. In truth, they construct reality out of air and fear. When a Basquiat or a Koons changes hands for $110 million, every other price drags along in its tidal wake. Not because the works have suddenly become aesthetically superior, but because a single number entered the game — hammered down on a wooden block in a millionaire's gallery.

  • Digitization extends reach — and with it, dependency on these three algorithms of taste.
  • Every online click amplifies the aura of untouchability; every live-stream bid binds the global audience deeper into the spell.
  • Conflicts of interest? Officially nonexistent, yet flirting behind every rostrum with the guarantee agreements.

The transparency these houses pretend to offer is in truth an instrument of exclusion. They legitimize value, but they also legitimize the inequality that makes it possible.

24,236 Reasons Not to Play Along

Here I have to laugh. Or cry. Maybe both. That strange feeling in the pit of your stomach when you realize you'd have to strike at the system 24,236 times to blow it up. I LAUGH YOU — that twitch between affection and contempt that lingers when you watch meaning get turned into speculation.

Imagine an artist paints himself. A face. A consciousness. A soul, if you like. And then he takes it apart. Not symbolically, not metaphorically, but literally — into 24,236 abstract fragments. Each piece a sliver of his skin, his colors, his existence. No trinity dictating the price. No monolithic hammer falling. Just 24,236 small decisions oscillating between $77 and $777. The fewer fragments remain, the more the last one costs. Not because it is more beautiful than the first. But because scarcity is the only real value in capitalism, even when the goods are pieces of a soul.

That is the poetics of dismemberment, far beyond the vanities of Mayfair.

The Insurance Game

The auction houses are the architects of a perfectly closed loop. They set the price, which then sets the insurance value, which then justifies the bank loan, which then finances the next purchase at — wouldn't you know it — the very same house. A self-fulfilling prophecy that eats itself like Ouroboros. And in the middle of this golden circle? The work itself, which wanted only one thing: to be looked at, to be experienced, to exist in the space between viewer and idea.

The Berlin Rebellion

There are attempts to break out of this logic. The Direkte Auktion in Berlin, for instance, where artists keep 66% of the hammer price and curators take 9% — a model that sidesteps the bloody food chain of gallery and auction house. A start, fragile but honest. Yet as long as the trinity dominates the global discourse, it remains a smear of color on a vast, abstract canvas no one can take in anymore.

The Final Hammer

In the end the uncomfortable question remains: do we want art that breathes, or art that yields a return? The great houses are not going to disappear. They are too powerful, too elegant, too deeply woven into the global flow of capital. But maybe — just maybe — we'll learn to laugh again. At the absurdity that three addresses define the taste of an entire species. At the notion that you can lock meaning into a safe like a piece of jewelry.

I LAUGH YOU. Because the alternative to laughter would be silent capitulation. And that costs more than any bid ever placed. Even if it were $777 million.
